title: Resources
text:
Where to begin

Bit by Bit — Matthew Salganik — the standard introduction to social research in the digital age, free to read online.
Summer Institutes in Computational Social Science — materials and recorded lectures from SICSS, openly available.
Text as Data — Grimmer, Roberts & Stewart — the reference for text-as-data methods in the social sciences.

title: Resources
text:
Methods and tutorials

statnet — R packages for network analysis and ERGMs, with tutorials.
NetLogo — agent-based modeling environment; the models library alone is worth reading.
The Effect — Nick Huntington-Klein — causal inference, free online.
Hugging Face — pretrained models, including Turkish-language ones such as BERTurk.

title: Resources
text:
Data sources

V-Dem — comparative measures of democracy, 1789 to present.
Correlates of War — interstate conflict, alliances, trade, and national capabilities.
TÜİK — Turkish Statistical Institute; national statistics and microdata.
İBB Açık Veri Portalı — Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality open data.

title: About the society
text: Boğaziçi University Computational Social Science Society

title: About the society
text:
What the society is for
Computational social science sits between disciplines, which means it is rarely anyone’s home department. A student in sociology who wants to learn network analysis, or one in computer engineering who wants to ask a substantive social question, often has nowhere obvious to go. The society exists to be that place: a standing group where methods are taught horizontally, between peers, rather than only vertically through coursework.

title: About the society
text:
How sessions work
We meet weekly during term. A typical session has one of three shapes:
Hands-on workshop. A member walks the group through a method with real data — fitting an ERGM, scraping a corpus, building a model in NetLogo. Everyone codes along.
Paper discussion. We read a recent methods or applications paper and work through what it actually did, including the parts the abstract glosses over.
Project session. Members present work in progress and get feedback. Several of the projects on our projects page started this way.

title: About the society
text:
Who can join
Anyone at Boğaziçi. There is no application and no prerequisite. Some members arrive already writing Python; others have never opened a terminal. Both are useful to have in the room, and the second group is why the workshops exist.

title: About the society
text:
Language
Sessions run in Turkish and English depending on who is present. Materials are usually in English, since that is where the literature is, but nobody is expected to present in a language they are uncomfortable with.

title: Projects
text:
Proposing a project
Bring it to a session. Projects that work well here tend to have a clear substantive question and a dataset that already exists — the constraint is usually analysis time, not ambition.

title: Computational Social Science Society
text:
Boğaziçi University




We are students and researchers at Boğaziçi University who study social questions with computational methods. We meet weekly for hands-on sessions, and we build things together — models, datasets, and small simulations anyone can run.

title: Computational Social Science Society
text:
Social questions, computational instruments
The society brings together people from political science, sociology, economics, history, and computer engineering. Our shared premise is that many social questions turn on processes we cannot observe directly — how opinions spread, how ties form, how what people say diverges from what they believe. Computational methods let us state those processes precisely and test them against data.
Sessions are informal and hands-on. Someone brings a problem or a paper, we work through the code together, and everyone leaves with something they can run. No prior programming experience is required to attend — several of our current members started with none.

title: Computational Social Science Society
text:
Come to a session
We meet weekly during term at the Department of Political Science and International Relations. Meetings are open — no membership form, no prerequisite. Bring a laptop if you have one.
Write to us at the address on the contact page and we will add you to the mailing list for meeting times and readings.
